analysis.body:
# US Grid Interconnection Queues: Implications for AI Data Center Power

Across five major regional grid operators, utilities are tracking 8,377 requests to connect 1.33 million megawatts of generation and storage waiting for grid interconnection as of mid-September 2026. This queue size reflects both the scale of energy demand growth—of which data centers are a significant driver—and the lag between when projects are proposed and when they can feed power to the network. The ERCOT queue in Texas alone represents 438,086 megawatts of requested capacity, while MISO covers the industrial heartland with 299,721 megawatts. These figures measure planned supply infrastructure, not data center consumption directly, but they indicate the infrastructure race underway to match rising loads.

Storage capacity in the queues—159,820 megawatts in ERCOT, 67,027 in MISO, 52,513 in Southwest Power Pool, and 46,870 in CAISO—totals roughly 326,230 megawatts and tracks closely with data center load patterns. Gas generation requests remain substantial across all regions, particularly in ERCOT (78,092 megawatts) and SPP (47,222 megawatts), though solar and wind dominate in absolute capacity terms. California's commercial electricity sales price of 27.33 dollars per megawatt-hour dwarfs Texas at 8.66 dollars, yet both states maintain deep interconnection backlogs, suggesting data center developers are willing to pay regional price premiums to access grid capacity near coastal tech hubs.

Commercial-sector sales across eight major data center states totaled 54,797.55 megawatt-hours in June 2026, a figure that serves as a proxy for combined data center and general commercial load but does not isolate AI workloads themselves. Texas leads absolute volume at 15,753.83 megawatt-hours, followed by California at 10,024.68, reflecting both region size and data center concentration. Watch the next quarterly EIA release and ERCOT monthly GIS report to track whether storage and gas requests continue accelerating relative to solar and wind, a marker of whether grid operators expect sustained, around-the-clock AI compute demand.
